title: NASA Astronaut Jessica Meir Shares Dazzling Moonlit Earth View From Space
excerpt: The Crew-12 commander posted the "Milky Way with a Moonlit Earth" clip on X days before her return from the International Space Station, calling it motivation for NASA's Artemis program.
body:
• NASA astronaut Jessica Meir posted a video on X showing the Milky Way over a moonlit Earth, captured from space during her Crew-12 mission.
  • "The Earth is so awash in Moonglow it looks like daytime, complete with blue oceans and continental outlines," she wrote, adding the sight is motivation "to return there with the NASA Artemis program."
  • Meir commands NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission alongside Jack Hathaway, Sophie Adenot and Andrey Fedyaev, who are due to undock on October 5 and splash down in the Pacific on October 6.
  • The post arrives as Crew-12 wraps up months of microgravity research, from cancer-drug crystallisation to quantum physics experiments.

NASA astronaut Jessica Meir gave Earth a look at itself from hundreds of miles up this week, sharing a video on X that shows the Milky Way hanging over a moonlit Earth. "The Earth is so awash in Moonglow it looks like daytime, complete with blue oceans and continental outlines," she wrote. "The Moon just keeps on giving even more motivation to return there with the NASA Artemis program."

The clip — which NDTV Profit reported was captured from the SpaceX Crew Dragon — was posted just days before Meir is due to return home, and quickly became one of the week's most shared images from orbit.

A mission drawing to a close

Meir commands NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission, which launched aboard a Dragon spacecraft on February 13 and docked with the International Space Station's Harmony module a day later. She is joined by NASA pilot Jack Hathaway, ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev, according to NASA.

The crew spent months running microgravity research designed to pay dividends on Earth. NASA says the mission included crystallising cancer-targeting treatments in orbit to better understand their properties, cooling and trapping atoms in the Cold Atom Lab to advance quantum technologies, and testing a wood-based bone scaffold that could one day protect astronauts and treat osteoporosis patients on Earth.

Heading home

The return is imminent. Crew-12 is expected to undock from the station on October 5 and splash down in the Pacific Ocean off Southern California on October 6, according to InterNewscast. Their replacements, NASA's SpaceX Crew-13, arrived on October 1 after a record-setting seven-hour, 55-minute Dragon flight, briefly bringing the station's population to 11.

"I think the thing that I'm looking forward to most is seeing my 3-and-a-half-year-old daughter."

— Jessica Meir, NASA astronaut

Meir said she is also eager to reconnect with the natural world — "feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves" — but will miss "being weightless all the time and the incredible views that we have."

The handover also underscores how thoroughly NASA now depends on SpaceX. Boeing's Starliner was grounded after its 2024 crew flight test suffered helium leaks and thruster failures, Tech Times reported, and NASA has since ordered six additional Dragon missions to cover what were intended to be Starliner flights — making Dragon the only American crew vehicle flying to the station through its planned retirement around 2030.

A familiar spark for the diaspora

Moments like Meir's moonlit video travel fast across the Indian diaspora, where Indian-origin astronauts — Sunita Williams most prominently — have turned NASA missions into shared community events. The spectacle doubles as inspiration: Meir's own framing of the video as motivation for Artemis reflects how these images recruit the next generation toward science and space.

What's next

Meir hands over command of the station to Roscosmos cosmonaut Pyotr Dubrov during a change-of-command ceremony on October 4 before the crew begins its journey home. Crew-13 will remain on orbit for roughly six months across Expeditions 75 and 76, continuing research on biology, materials science and human physiology in space. And the Moon that lit up Meir's video remains the next destination: NASA's Artemis program is working toward returning astronauts to the lunar surface, the first step toward the deep-space missions Crew-12's research is meant to enable.
